explanations.explanation: Steady it is. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, says, “Your words have steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). He adds that Job braced knees that were buckling. So Job was the one folks leaned on when their legs went wobbly, and that's a great thing to be known for.

Scold sounds like a finger-wagging lecture, but that's not what Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, says. He says Job's words “steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). Job lifted people up instead of lecturing them. I'd take a friend like that any day of the week.

Scatter is how my sprinkles behave when I bump the jar, not how Job treated people. Eliphaz, one of Job's three friends, says Job's words “steadied those who stumbled…” (Job 4:4). Job's words held people together. He also strengthened feeble hands and braced buckling knees, so he was the opposite of a scatterer.

That's it. Eliphaz asks, “Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?” (Job 4:6). He's pointing Job back to his own reverence and his upright ways. Notice it's phrased as a question, so Eliphaz is nudging Job to lean on them.

Pride isn't the word Eliphaz uses. He asks, “Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?” (Job 4:6). He's talking about where Job should rest his confidence and his hope. Nothing in the verse mentions bragging.

Keeping quiet isn't what Eliphaz is asking for here. He asks, “Is your reverence not your confidence, and the uprightness of your ways your hope?” (Job 4:6). He's saying those things should be Job's confidence and hope. It's about where Job puts his trust, and silence never comes up.

Right on target. Eliphaz pleads, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (Job 4:7). He's asking Job to think about whether he's ever seen that happen. Eliphaz is making his case, and it's the question his whole speech leans on.

Kings never show up in this verse. Eliphaz pleads with Job, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (Job 4:7). His question is about the innocent and the upright. Crowns and thrones aren't on his mind.

Nobody's checking bank accounts in this verse. Eliphaz pleads, “Who, being innocent, has ever perished? Or where have the upright been destroyed?” (Job 4:7). The question is about whether the innocent and upright ever perish. Happiness of the wealthy isn't part of it.

Reap is the word. Eliphaz says, “As I have observed, those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same.” (Job 4:8). It's a farming picture: what you plant is what comes up. Eliphaz says he observed this himself, and I think he's counting on Job to nod along.

Lose sounds close, but it isn't what Eliphaz says. He says those who plow iniquity and sow trouble “reap the same” (Job 4:8). Reaping belongs to the farm, where you gather what you planted. So the trouble they sow is the trouble they gather.

Escape is the opposite of what Eliphaz says. He says, “…those who plow iniquity and those who sow trouble reap the same.” (Job 4:8). Reaping means gathering what you planted, so nobody slips out the back door. Eliphaz says he observed it himself.

Yes. Eliphaz says, “By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.” (Job 4:9). That's his claim about those who sow trouble. It's what Eliphaz says, so we're hearing it from his mouth.

No enemies with swords in this verse. Eliphaz says, “By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.” (Job 4:9). He names God's breath and the blast of His anger. Swords don't come into it.
A flood isn't in Eliphaz's words here. He says, “By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of His anger they are consumed.” (Job 4:9). The breath of God is what he names. No water, no waves.

The lions in Eliphaz's picture don't end up strong and fed. He says, “The lion may roar, and the fierce lion may growl, yet the teeth of the young lions are broken.” (Job 4:10). Then, “The old lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.” (Job 4:11). All that roaring, and it ends with broken teeth, no prey and scattered cubs.

Right, false. Eliphaz says, “The lion may roar, and the fierce lion may growl, yet the teeth of the young lions are broken.” (Job 4:10). The old lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered (Job 4:11). That's a lot of noise for a sad ending.

Calm and peaceful is not how Eliphaz describes it. He says, “fear and trembling came over me and made all my bones shudder.” (Job 4:14). That's a whole body shaking. Nobody shudders to the bones during a nice nap.
False is right. Eliphaz says, “fear and trembling came over me and made all my bones shudder.” (Job 4:14). There's no peace in that sentence. Even his bones were in on the shaking.

He couldn't make it out. Eliphaz says the spirit “stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form loomed before my eyes…” (Job 4:16). So it stopped moving, and he still couldn't tell what he was looking at. Standing still didn't make it any clearer.

False is right. Eliphaz says it “stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form loomed before my eyes…” (Job 4:16). He saw a form, but he couldn't tell what it looked like. Then came a whispering voice.

explanations.answer: If a mortal can be more righteous than God
explanations.explanation: That's the question. The voice asks, “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” (Job 4:17). It's whispered, and it's the heart of what Eliphaz heard that night. Eliphaz gives it as the voice's question to Job.

explanations.answer: If a mortal can see God and still live
explanations.explanation: Seeing God isn't what the voice asks. It asks, “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” (Job 4:17). The question is about being more righteous and more pure. Nobody in this verse is looking at God.

explanations.answer: If a mortal can count all the stars
explanations.explanation: No stargazing here. The voice asks, “Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or a man more pure than his Maker?” (Job 4:17). It's a question about righteousness and purity. Stars never come up.

explanations.answer: People fall even shorter than angels
explanations.explanation: You've got the point. The voice says, “If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay…” (Job 4:18-19). It's a step-up argument: if that's said of angels, then how much more of people. The voice is stacking the comparison against people.

explanations.answer: People are more trusted than angels
explanations.explanation: The voice goes the other way. It says, “If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay…” (Job 4:18-19). The words “how much more” push the point onto people, and not in a flattering direction. People are called houses of clay, with foundations in the dust.

explanations.answer: People are just as pure as angels
explanations.explanation: Just as pure would make the voice's argument fall apart. It says, “If God puts no trust in His servants, and He charges His angels with error, how much more those who dwell in houses of clay…” (Job 4:18-19). “How much more” means people come off even worse than the angels in that picture. The voice describes them as living in houses of clay.

True. The voice says, “They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever.” (Job 4:20). The word “unnoticed” is right there. It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth letting it sit for a second.

The text says otherwise. The voice says, “They are smashed to pieces from dawn to dusk; unnoticed, they perish forever.” (Job 4:20). “Unnoticed” is the very word it uses. It's a heavy line, and I think it hurts to read.
The text says the opposite. Eliphaz says the fool's sons are “crushed in court without a defender.” (Job 5:4). Nobody stands up for them. Courtroom, no lawyer, and that's his picture.
False is right. Eliphaz says the fool's sons “are far from safety, crushed in court without a defender.” (Job 5:4). Nobody stands up for them in that courtroom. It's a lonely scene.

That's right. Eliphaz says, “The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.” (Job 5:5). They take it even from the thorns, so they're not leaving anything behind. That fool's harvest is long gone.

Nothing rots in this verse. Eliphaz says, “The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns…” (Job 5:5). People take it, and they even reach into the thorns to do it. Nobody's leaving a crumb.

No locusts are mentioned here. Eliphaz says, “The hungry consume his harvest, taking it even from the thorns, and the thirsty pant after his wealth.” (Job 5:5). The ones taking the harvest are the hungry. The thirsty are panting after his wealth too.

The text says the opposite. Eliphaz says, “For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground.” (Job 5:6). Trouble doesn't pop up out of the dirt like a weed. Then he goes on to say where he thinks it does come from.

False is right. Eliphaz says, “For distress does not spring from the dust, and trouble does not sprout from the ground.” (Job 5:6). So no, trouble doesn't come up like a seedling. It's a short verse, but it sets up what he says next.
Yes. Eliphaz says, “However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him.” (Job 5:8). That's his advice to Job. He doesn't say anything about elders or anyone else.

explanations.answer: Take his case to the elders
explanations.explanation: No elders in this verse. Eliphaz says, “However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him.” (Job 5:8). He'd take it straight to God. That's the advice he gives.

Packing up isn't part of his advice. Eliphaz says, “However, if I were you, I would appeal to God and lay my cause before Him.” (Job 5:8). Job is a man from the land of Uz (Job 1:1), and Eliphaz never tells him to leave. He tells him to appeal to God.
Lowly is it. Eliphaz says, “He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety.” (Job 5:11). The ones who were down get lifted up. That's good news for anyone who's felt low.

Proud doesn't fit this verse. Eliphaz says, “He sets the lowly on high, so that mourners are lifted to safety.” (Job 5:11). It's the lowly who get set on high. The mourners get lifted to safety right along with them.

The crafty show up a verse later, and it goes differently for them. Eliphaz says, “He thwarts the schemes of the crafty, so that their hands find no success.” (Job 5:12). But the one set on high in verse 11 is the lowly. Mourners are lifted to safety too.

Corrects is it. Eliphaz says, “Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.” (Job 5:17). He tells Job not to despise that discipline. Correction isn't fun, but Eliphaz calls the man who receives it blessed.

Rewards sounds nice, but it isn't the word. Eliphaz says, “Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects…” (Job 5:17). Correction is the word he picks. He follows it with “so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.”

Spares isn't what Eliphaz says. He says, “Blessed indeed is the man whom God corrects; so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty.” (Job 5:17). The blessing is tied to being corrected. He's telling Job not to despise it.

True. Eliphaz says, “For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.” (Job 5:18). Both halves are in the same verse. The wounding and striking come first, and then the binding and healing.

The text says it's true. Eliphaz says, “For He wounds, but He also binds; He strikes, but His hands also heal.” (Job 5:18). The wounding and striking are paired with binding and healing. It's all in one verse.

Laugh is it. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.” (Job 5:22). That's quite a promise to make to a man who has lost so much. Whatever you think of Eliphaz's words, the laughing is what he says.

Hiding isn't in his promise. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.” (Job 5:22). Job won't be ducking behind anything in that picture. He'll be laughing.

Praying against them isn't what Eliphaz says. He tells Job, “You will laugh at destruction and famine, and need not fear the beasts of the earth.” (Job 5:22). The verse is about laughing and not fearing. It doesn't say what Job will do in prayer.

The text says the opposite. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth.” (Job 5:25). Many, and like grass, which covers the whole field. Few is not in his promise.

False is right. Eliphaz tells Job, “You will know that your offspring will be many, your descendants like the grass of the earth.” (Job 5:25). Like the grass of the earth means a lot of them. Eliphaz is painting a full house.

Full vigor is it. Eliphaz says, “You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.” (Job 5:26). Grain gathered in season is ripe and ready. That's the picture he gives Job.

Honor is a nice thought, but it isn't what Eliphaz says. He says, “You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.” (Job 5:26). The word is vigor, meaning strength. The grain is gathered right in season.

That's the opposite of his picture. Eliphaz says, “You will come to the grave in full vigor, like a sheaf of grain gathered in season.” (Job 5:26). Just before that, he says Job's descendants will be many (Job 5:25). Full vigor is how he says Job will arrive.
